titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — Epilogue I: the just laws (xl 1 – xli 74)
part: Epilogue I · the just laws (Col. xl 1 – xli 74)
about: The first part of the epilogue, which the stele carries after the last numbered law. It opens by saying what has gone before: these are the just decisions that Hammurabi, the capable king, established, by which he made the land hold to a firm way and good leadership (xl 1–8). The king then speaks of himself in the first person: the perfect king, to whom Ellil and Marduk gave the black-headed people to shepherd; he was not careless; with the weapon of Zamama and Ishtar, the wisdom of Ea and the power of Marduk he tore out the enemy above and below, put out the wars, and made the people lie down in safety (xl 9–41). He is the shepherd whose scepter is straight, whose good shade is spread over his city, who held Sumer and Akkad in his bosom; the strong may not wrong the weak, and the orphan and the widow are to be done right by (xl 42–69). To judge the cases of the land he wrote his weighty words on his stele and set it up before his statue, “King of Justice” (xl 70–78); he is pre-eminent among the city-kings, and by the command of Shamash he prays that justice may appear in the land and, by the word of Marduk, that no one efface his designs (xl 79–94). Column xli turns to the reader. A wronged man is to come before the statue, read the stele aloud, hear the words, see his case, and pray for the king, saying that Hammurabi was like a father to the people, revered Marduk’s word, won the victory, gladdened Marduk’s heart and set the land right; the guardian spirits and the gods of Esagila are to show favor before Marduk and Zarpanitum (xli 1–58). Then comes the charge to the king of the future: keep the words of justice written on my stele, and do not change the judgments and decisions I gave or efface my designs (xli 59–74; the charge continues in the next part). The numbers in the margin are the stele’s own line numbers, not law numbers. A few readings are uncertain; the notes say where (the ūsam/nūram of xl 21, aḫḫiša, īša, igirrê, danītam, the signs for “statue” and “brick”). Where the print alone does not show how Harper divides the lines (xl 65–69, xl 90–94, xli 25–33), the plate’s ruled lines confirm his division.

sentences.l: The-judgments of-justice which Hammurabi the-king the-capable established-and,
sentences.i: The just decisions that Hammurabi, the capable king, established,
sentences.n: The epilogue begins here, in a new column (xl). It opens like a heading: a noun phrase with no main verb of its own, “the judgments of justice” (dīnāt, the plural “judgments” in the form that stands before a genitive; mīšarim, “of justice”, genitive). The relative particle ša “which” then opens a clause about Hammurabi: ukīnūma is ukīn, the D-stem of kânum “to be firm” (D: “to make firm, to establish”), with the subjunctive -u that every verb in a ša-clause takes, and -ma “and”, which hooks this clause to the next unit. lēʾûm “capable, mighty” (Harper’s li-u-um; the litany spells the same word li-i-a-um). The king names himself in the third person here and moves to “I” at xl 9. Harper’s square brackets (as in later lines: wa-[aš]-tu-tim) mark signs he restores or is unsure of; I keep them in the signs.

sentences.l: the-land right-conduct firm and guidance good caused-to-take-hold.
sentences.i: and caused the land to take hold of a firm right way and good leadership.
sentences.n: The relative clause goes on: ušaṣbitu is the Š-stem (causative) of ṣabātum “to seize”, 3rd singular, again with the subjunctive -u: “he made (the land) seize”. A Š verb takes two accusatives, here three words in -am in a row: mātam “the land” is the one made to seize, and ūsam kīnam “a firm right way” and rīdam damqam “good leadership” are what it seizes. ūsum is Harper’s “help, assistance, support” (he lists this place, xl 21 and the prologue’s u-si-im under it); in the prologue and the litany we render it “right conduct” (compare the litany’s mātam ūsim šuḫuzim, “to give the land right conduct”), and I keep that here. rīdum is Harper’s ridu “government”, a noun of redûm “to lead”. damqam is Harper’s dam-ga-am (his damku “pure”): the usual word is damqum “good”, with q written by the GA sign. Uncertain: Harper’s u-sa-am has no caron visible on the page (our transcription of Harper’s print notes that it might be u-ša-am); the plate shows the SA sign, and ūsam is the word one expects in this phrase.

sentences.l: Hammurabi — the-king the-perfect — I(-am).
sentences.i: I am Hammurabi, the perfect king.
sentences.n: Here the king speaks in the first person, and that voice runs through the whole epilogue. This is a sentence with no verb: the name, the titles, and the pronoun anāku “I” held back to the end for emphasis (the Akkadian order is “Hammurabi, the perfect king — I”). gitmālum “perfect, complete” is the title the litany gave the king (mu-uš-ta-lum gi-it-ma-lum); Harper’s glossary has gitmalu “perfect”. This is the first of many lines of royal self-praise (“I am the shepherd who …”).

sentences.l: to the-black-headed which Ellil gave-me, their-shepherding Marduk gave-me,
sentences.i: To the black-headed people whom Ellil gave me, and whose shepherding Marduk gave me,
sentences.n: This phrase is fronted: the king’s main verbs come in the next unit (“I was not careless”). SAG.GI₆ is a Sumerogram (a word written with Sumerian signs and read in Akkadian): it stands for ṣalmāt qaqqadim, “the black-headed people”, that is, mankind (our house rendering). Harper prints it SAG.GIG and reads it the same way; the plate sign after SAG is the MI sign, as in the prologue. {d}EN.LÍL is Ellil, the divine determinative {d} (the AN sign, read nothing) in front of the name; Harper calls him Bêl, “lord”, and his glossary gives “Bêl [EN.LIL]”. išrukam is išruk “he gave (as a gift)” (šarākum) plus the ventive -am “to me”, and iddinam is iddin “he gave” (nadānum) plus -am. ša marks the relative clause “whom (Ellil gave me)”. rēʾūssina is rēʾûtum “shepherdship, rule” (Harper: “government, guardianship”) plus -šina “their”, the ssi spelled with the ZI sign.

sentences.l: not I-was-careless; my-arm not I-let-drop.
sentences.i: I was not careless, and I did not let my arm drop (I was never idle).
sentences.n: Two short denials of the king’s own conduct, each with ul “not” before the verb. egû is from egûm “to be careless, to neglect” (Harper’s e-gu, 1st person “I was careless”; compare itēgi in the laws). aḫī ul addi is “I did not let my arm drop”: aḫī is aḫum “arm” with -ī “my” (Harper files a-ḫi under aḫu “side”), and addi is “I threw, let fall” (nadûm). It is the idiom you met in the laws, aḫšu iddi “he let his arm drop”, which means he was idle (§44); here it is first person and negative: “I was never idle”.

sentences.l: places of-peace I-sought-for-them; straits difficult I-opened-up; support I-brought-out-for-them.
sentences.i: I sought out places of peace for them; I opened up the difficult straits; I brought out help for them.
sentences.n: Three first-person clauses with no connecting “and” (the style of the self-praise). ešteʾišināšim: ešteʾi is the perfect “I have sought” of šeʾûm (the perfect, with the -t- after the first root letter; Harper’s I,2), plus the dative -šināšim “for them” (feminine plural, agreeing with ṣalmāt “the black-headed”, which is feminine plural). upetti is the D-stem of petûm “to open”, 1st person (Harper’s u-[pi]-it-ti); pušqī “straits, tight places” (Harper’s pusku) with waštūtim “difficult, steep” (Harper’s wastu). ušēṣi is the Š of waṣûm “to go out”: “I made go out, I brought out”; the Š and the pronoun are written together. Uncertain: ūsam. Harper prints [u]-si-am “help, support” (the same word as xl 6, where we say “right way”), but his own footnote 1 says “Better to read with Winckler, [nu-r]a-am”, i.e. nūram “light”; the litany has mušēṣi nūrim “who makes light rise”, a close parallel. On the plate the first sign is drawn in outline (damaged), so it is a restoration either way, and the next two signs are drawn whole; I keep Harper’s ūsam and give Winckler’s as the alternative (“I brought out light for them”).

sentences.l: with-the-weapon mighty which Zamama and Ishtar entrusted-to-me,
sentences.i: with the mighty weapon that Zamama and Ishtar entrusted to me,
sentences.n: ina + noun is “with, by means of”, and what follows is another relative clause with ša. GIŠ.TUKUL is the Sumerogram for kakkum “weapon” (GIŠ “wood” plus a second sign; Harper prints only kakku and the glossary gives no spelling); the plate shows two signs there with no ending, the second a box with horizontal strokes like Harper’s List of Signs no. 187 (ku, tuk), which is our TUK; whether the scribe meant the sign TUKUL by it is not checked (TENTATIVE). The first is the wide GIŠ sign that also stands in GIŠ.PA-šu (xl 44). dannim is “mighty” (dannum, as in the prologue, “the strong”). Zamama is the war-god of Kish. Harper prints {ilu}ZA.MA(L).MA(L); I spell it as in the litany. {d}INANNA is Ištar: Harper reads the same sign Nanâ (“Ishtar of Uruk”), and I keep our usual Ištar. ušatlimūnim is the Š-stem of talāmum, which Harper glosses “to entrust” (a rare verb), with the ventive -nim “to me” and the plural -ū: “they (the two gods) entrusted to me”.

sentences.l: with-the-wisdom which Ea decreed-for-me, with-the-power which Marduk gave-me,
sentences.i: with the wisdom that Ea decreed for me, with the power that Marduk gave me,
sentences.n: The same “ina + noun + relative clause” pattern, twice. IGI.GÁL-im is igigallim, a Sumerogram (“wide of eye”) for “wisdom”; Harper normalizes it egigalim and glosses igigallu “intelligent, broad of vision”; the litany has the same word (mu-di IGI.GÁL-im “who knows wisdom”). {d}EN.KI is Ea, god of wisdom. išīmam is išīm “he decreed” (šâmum “to fix, decree”, the same verb that fixes destinies in the prologue; not the “buy” šâmum) plus the ventive -am “to me”. līʾūtim is “power, might” (Harper’s liʾūtu), the noun belonging to lēʾûm “capable” (xl 4). Our transcription of Harper’s print notes that the sixth letter of his egigalim is faint; the plate row has five signs, which fits i-na IGI.GÁL-im (confirmed).

sentences.l: enemies above and below I-tore-out, battles I-extinguished, the-flesh of-the-land I-made-good.
sentences.i: I tore out the enemies above and below, I put out the wars, and I made the land prosper.
sentences.n: A run of first-person verbs with nothing between them. assuḫ is “I tore out, uprooted” (nasāḫum), the verb the laws use of casting a son out of the family; it is written az-zu-uḫ, with the z-signs doing duty for s (Harper reads azzuḫ). elîš and šaplîš “above” and “below” (the ending -iš makes an adverb) together mean “everywhere”. qablātim “battles” is Harper’s gablu “battle”; the first sign GA is read qa₂, since the word is qablum. ubelli is the D-stem of balûm (Harper: I “to destroy”, II “to extinguish, to make an end of”): “I put out”. šīr mātim uṭīb is “the flesh of the land I made good”, the same phrase as the litany’s šīr nišī uṭīb (the prologue has ana šīr nišī ṭubbim); šīrum “flesh” here means bodily well-being, and ṭâbum D is “to make good”.

sentences.l: the-people of-the-settlements in-safety I-made-lie-down; a-molester not I-let-have-them.
sentences.i: I made the people of the settlements lie down in safety, and I let no one harass them.
sentences.n: dadmī is “of the settlements, inhabited places” (Harper’s dadmu), in the genitive after nišī “people of”. ušarbiṣ is the Š-stem of rabāṣum “to lie down” (Harper: “to make to rest”): “I made lie down”; aburrī “in safety, secure” is Harper’s aburru “security, safety”, which I take as an adverb (the ending is not explained by the grammar). mugallitam is a participle, “one who molests, terrifies” (Harper’s galatu II “to molest”), in the accusative. ušaršišināti is the Š of rašûm “to get, have” (“to let get”, Harper’s “grant, allow”) plus -šināti “them”: “I did not let them get a molester”, that is, I allowed no one to harass them.

sentences.l: The-gods great called-me-and,
sentences.i: The great gods called me, and
sentences.n: DINGIR (the AN sign alone) “god” and GAL.GAL “great” (the sign doubled) are Sumerograms read as the plural ilāni rabûti, “the great gods” (the same two words as in the litany: DINGIR.DINGIR GAL.GAL). ibbûninnima: ibbû “they named, called” (nabûm, as in the prologue, “they called my name”), -ninni “me” (the object suffix -anni, with the doubled n that the object suffix often takes after a vowel), and -ma “and”. Here the king says it was the gods who called him to the kingship; the -ma joins this clause to the self-description that follows.

sentences.l: I-indeed the-shepherd the-keeper-safe whose-scepter is-straight,
sentences.i: I am the shepherd, the protector, whose scepter is straight;
sentences.n: anākuma is anāku “I” with -ma, which here stresses the subject: “I indeed”. SIPA is the Sumerogram (PA plus LU) for rēʾûm “shepherd”, the picture of the king for his people. mušallimum is a D participle of šalāmum “to be whole”, so “one who keeps whole, safeguards” (Harper’s glossary: “guardian, protecting”). GIŠ.PA-šu is ḫaṭṭašu “his scepter” (GIŠ “wood” + PA, a staff; Harper prints ḫaṭṭu-šu); the stem sits in the Sumerogram, so the suffix -šu “his” is the only syllable written. The clause ša ḫaṭṭašu išarat “whose scepter is straight” is a first example of the “whose … ” construction: ša, then a noun with its own possessive suffix, then the verb. išarat is from ešērum “to be straight, right”, 3rd person feminine (the scepter is “straight”, which also means “just”).

sentences.l: my-shade good over my-city is-spread;
sentences.i: my good shade is spread over my city;
sentences.n: ṣillī “my shade, my protection” (Harper’s silu “protection”; the final -ī is “my”) with ṭābum “good”, and the verb tariṣ “it is spread out” (tarāṣum “to spread out”, Harper). The king’s protection is pictured as shade falling over the city. URU-ia is ālīya “my city” (URU the Sumerogram for ālum; ia “my” written out), which here means Babylon. ana “to, over”.

sentences.l: in my-bosom the-people of-the-land of-Sumer and of-Akkad I-held,
sentences.i: I held the people of Sumer and Akkad in my bosom;
sentences.n: utlīya “my bosom, lap” (Harper’s utlu “bosom, side”): the king holds his people as a parent holds a child. nišī māt Šumerim u Akkadim is “the people of the land of Sumer and Akkad”: nišī “people of” (a form that stands before a genitive) and mātim (here written with the bare Sumerogram KALAM, read māt, the form before a genitive), then the two names in the genitive. Sumer and Akkad are south and north Babylonia. ukīl is “I held, carried, provided for” (kullum, Harper’s kalu II “to carry, to provide for”).

sentences.l: by my-guardian-spirit, aḫḫiša(?), in peace I-carried-them,
sentences.i: By my guardian spirit I carried them along in peace,
sentences.n: lamassīya is “my guardian spirit” (lamassum, the protective genius that goes with a person; Harper: “a genius, guardian spirit”). attabbalšināti is “I carried them”: attabbal is tabālum “to carry, take” in the Gt stem (Harper: I,2), plus -šināti “them”; šulmim “peace, well-being”. Uncertain: aḫḫiša. Harper’s glossary files it under aḫu “brother” (with aḫḫūša, aḫḫīša “his/her brothers”), which I cannot fit into the sentence from the grammar, so it stays untranslated in the English (“side by side, like brothers” would be a guess).

sentences.l: by my-wisdom I-sheltered-them.
sentences.i: by my wisdom I kept them safe.
sentences.n: nemēqīya “my wisdom” (Harper’s nemequ, written with the KI sign read qi₂). uštapṣiršināti is the Š-stem perfect (Harper’s III,2) of paṣārum plus -šināti “them”; Harper glosses paṣāru “to hide, to restrain” (cf. pazāru), and I render it “kept safe, sheltered” (UNCERTAIN: the exact sense of this stem is not clear to me, and “sheltered”, “protected” and “restrained” all fit).

sentences.l: the-strong the-weak to not wronging, the-bereft the-widow to-set-right,
sentences.i: so that the strong might not wrong the weak, to do right by the orphan and the widow,
sentences.n: This is the prologue’s phrase again: dannum enšam ana lā ḫabālim, “so that the strong might not wrong the weak” (our house rendering): ana + infinitive “in order to (do)”, with lā “not” before the infinitive, and the two sides placed first (“the strong, the weak”). NU.TUK and NU.MU.SU are Sumerograms: literally “the one who has not” and “the one with no husband”; Harper reads them ekûtu and almattu, the “orphan” and “widow” (almattum is certain; ekûtam “bereft, orphan” is UNCERTAIN). Both stand with no Akkadian ending, and I supply -am (accusative) because they are the objects of the infinitive. šūtešurim is the Št-stem infinitive of ešērum “to be straight”: “to set right, to guide aright” (as in the prologue). The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.l: in Babylon, the-city whose its-head Anum and Ellil raised-high, in Esagila,
sentences.i: in Babylon, the city whose head Anum and Ellil raised high, in Esagila,
sentences.n: KÁ.DINGIR.RA{ki} is Bābilim “of Babylon” (“gate of the god”), with the place determinative {ki}; Harper prints KA.DINGIR.RA.KI. URU is ālum “city”, in apposition to Babylon; the relative clause ša … rēšīšu ullû “whose head they raised” is another “whose …” construction, with the verb last. ullû is the D of elûm “to go up”: “they raised high” (Harper’s “to raise on high”), 3rd plural; the two subjects are the high gods. AN is the bare AN sign (the plate shows the same star as the determinative), read Anum, the sky-god, as in the prologue and the litany: Harper prints ilim “a god” (his glossary files this line under ilu), but the pair with Ellil (Harper’s Bêl, here {d}EN.LÍL) points to Anum, and as one of the two subjects of ullû it is nominative. Esagila is Marduk’s great temple in Babylon. On the plate xl 65, 66 and 67 are separate ruled lines (ri-ši-šu / u-ul-lu-u / i-na Esagila), so Harper’s division stands.

sentences.l: of-the-house which like heaven and earth its-foundations firm(-are),
sentences.i: the house whose foundations are as firm as heaven and earth,
sentences.n: bītim “of the house” (the Sumerogram É, with no ending written) stands in apposition to Esagila: “in Esagila, the house …”. The rest is the prologue’s simile, kīma šamê u erṣetim (“like heaven and earth”) for something firmly founded (there it was Marduk’s kingship). išdāšu “its foundations” is the Sumerogram SUḪUŠ “foundation” plus -šu “its”; Harper’s glossary has išdi-šu at this place and his transliteration išda-šu; I read the dual išdāšu, because the verb ends in -ā, the dual (or feminine plural) ending of the stative: kīnā, from kânum “to be firm”, “are firm” (the prologue has the same noun in the feminine, išdāša). On the plate xl 68 and 69 are single ruled lines, each with a second row (Harper’s {b}), as he prints them.

sentences.l: the-case of-the-land to-judge, the-decisions of-the-land to-decide, the-wronged to-set-right, my-words weighty
sentences.i: To judge the cases of the land, to give decisions for the land, to put right the wronged: my weighty words
sentences.n: Three purposes, each an infinitive (the first two after ana, the third, šūtešurim, standing without its own ana): dīānim “to judge” (dīānum), parāsim “to decide” (parāsum), šūtešurim “to set right”. The objects come first: dīn mātim “the case(s) of the land” (dīnum, as in the laws), purussê mātim “the decisions of the land” (purussûm “decision”; the plural form purussê stands before the genitive), and ḫablim “the wronged one” (ḫablum, from ḫabālum “to wrong”, the verb of “the strong might not wrong the weak”). All of this leads to “my weighty words”, which is what the next unit says he did with them. awâtīya is awâtu “words” (plural of awātum) plus -ia “my”. šūqurātim: Harper reads šu-ku-ra-tim “weighty” (his šukuru); I read the KU sign as qu₂, which gives šūqurātim “precious, weighty” (UNCERTAIN, but the sense is the same).

sentences.l: on my-stele I-wrote-and, before my-statue, king of-justice, I-set-up.
sentences.i: I wrote them on my stele, and I set it up before my statue, “King of Justice”.
sentences.n: narûya “my stele” (narûm “stele”, Harper’s naru “monument, inscription”), aštur is “I wrote” (šaṭārum) and -ma “and”. Here the king says what the stele is: his words, and before it a statue of him called šar mīšarim “King of Justice”. ukīn is “I set up, established” (the D of kânum, the verb of xl 5); the thing set up (the stele) is understood. ṣalmīya “my statue”: the Sumerogram for ṣalmum “statue, image” (Harper’s salmu) plus ia “my”. The sign I give it, ALAN, is only a TENTATIVE match: Harper’s glossary does not spell the word. In šar mīšarim, LUGAL (šar) is the bare Sumerogram and mīšarim is spelled out. ina maḫar “before, in the presence of” (maḫar, as in the laws).

sentences.l: The-king who among the-kings-of-the-city pre-eminent I(-am); my-words weighty(-are); (in)-power a-rival not has-(?)
sentences.i: I am the king who stands out among the city-kings; my words are weighty; in power I have no rival.
sentences.n: šarrum ša ina šar ālim šūturu anāku: a noun with a relative clause, then the pronoun at the end, as in xl 10. LUGAL.URU is Harper’s šar+alim, “king of the city” (the + joins two signs), read as in the litany, where the plural sense “city-kings” is marked uncertain. šūturu is a stative (“is surpassing”; Harper: šuturu “pre-eminent”; watārum Š). našqā is “weighty, choice” (Harper’s našku, with the GA sign read qa₂), stative plural of the subject awâtūa “my words”. Uncertain: līʾūti šāninam ul īša. Harper reads it “(my) power has no rival” (šananu “to rival”, līʾūti “power”, išû “to have”). The carver wrote NA where ŠA was meant; Harper’s i-na(=ša) corrects it to īša, which I keep, but the form (I would expect īšu, “he has”) is not one I can account for from the grammar. The subject is not clear either; I read the clause as “in power I have no rival”.

sentences.l: By the-command of-Shamash, the-judge great of-heaven and earth, justice in the-land may-it-be-made-to-appear,
sentences.i: By the command of Shamash, the great judge of heaven and earth, may justice be made to appear in the land,
sentences.n: First wish in this passage, marked by the prefix li-: lištēpi is li + the Št-stem of wapûm “to appear” (the Š-stem šūpûm is “to make appear”, as in the prologue’s “to make justice appear in the land”, our house rendering); the Št makes it a passive: “let it be made to appear”. Harper’s li-iš-te-bi is listed as a III,2 form; I take it with the verb “to appear” (UNCERTAIN: his glossary entry is cut off at the top of the page, but it lists šūpê’im (prologue) and mušēpi (litany) beside it), with bi standing for pi₂. ina kibīt “by the command of” (kibītum, Harper’s kibitu “speech, command”; the word is written ki-be-it). {d}UTU is Šamaš, the sun-god, god of justice and “judge” (dajjānum). šamê and erṣetim “heaven” and “earth” are the Sumerograms AN and KI with no endings (Harper’s šamê [AN], irṣitim [KI]). Uncertain: mīšari, written without the final -m: Harper normalizes mīšari, and the word could be “my justice” (mīšarī) or the plain noun; I translate “justice”.

sentences.l: By the-word of-Marduk my-lord, my-designs an-effacer not-may-they-get.
sentences.i: By the word of Marduk my lord, may my designs never acquire anyone to efface them;
sentences.n: The divine word that authorizes the stele: ina awāt Marduk bēlīya “by the word of Marduk my lord” (awātum). uṣurātūa is “my designs, images” (Harper’s uṣurtu “relief, statue”; uṣurātu is the plural, ūa is “my”): here the carved text and picture of the stele. The sentence is a negative wish. a (Harper: “prohibitive particle”; I write ay) before a verb in the preterite means “may (it) not”: here ir-ši-a, iršiā, from rašûm “to get” (Harper’s ir-ši-a): the ending -ā is the 3rd feminine plural, agreeing with the feminine plural uṣurātūa (the ventive -am would be written -am); it takes the king’s “designs” as subject and mušazziqam “one who effaces” (Harper’s nazaku III “to cut off, efface, destroy”; the Š participle, with the KAM sign read qam) as object: “may my designs not get an effacer”. Uncertain: the stem and root of the participle.

sentences.l: in Esagila which I-love, my-name in favor
sentences.i: in Esagila, which I love, may my name, with favor,
sentences.n: The wish about the name begins here and its verb stands at the head of the next column (xli 2), because a unit never crosses a column. arâmmu “I love” (râmum) with the subjunctive -u, because it sits in a ša-clause; the relative ša has Esagila as its object and no pronoun to repeat it. šumī “my name”. ina damiqtim “in favor, graciously” (damiqtum, a noun, Harper’s damiqtu “grace, favor”; the q is written with the IG sign). On the plate line 94 is one ruled line with a second row (Harper’s {b} before šumī marks the break), so it is one stele line.

sentences.l: for eternity may-it-be-named.
sentences.i: be spoken of for ever.
sentences.n: ana dār “for ever” (dārum “duration”; compare dāriš “forever” in the litany). lizzakir is li + izzakir, the N-stem (passive) of zakārum “to name, mention” (Harper’s IV,1): “may it be named, be mentioned”. Together with xl 93–94: “in Esagila, which I love, may my name be spoken of with favor for ever.” The prefix li- (“let, may”) is the sign of the 3rd person wish; it will be everywhere in what follows.

sentences.l: A-man wronged who a-matter has,
sentences.i: Any wronged man who has a case
sentences.n: From here the king speaks to the reader. awīlum is “a man” (the word that opens the laws); ḫablum “wronged” (ḫabālum). ša awātam iraššû: “who has a matter”, awātum “word, matter, lawsuit” and iraššû, the present of rašûm “to get, to have” with the subjunctive -u, as in the laws (“a man who has a claim”). The wronged man is placed first, like a subject hung out in front, and is picked up by the verb in the next unit. The case is his own.

sentences.l: to before my-statue, king of-justice, may-he-go-and,
sentences.i: let him come before my statue, “King of Justice”, and
sentences.n: lillikma is li + illik, the preterite of alākum “to go”, with -ma “and”: “let him go, and”. The prefix li- + the shape of the preterite makes a wish or command in the 3rd person (the precative; first seen at xl 84). The -ma joins the commands in a chain: let him go, and read, and hear, and let it show him. ana maḫar ṣalmīya “to the presence of my statue”, with the statue’s name šar mīšarim as at xl 76–77. The king tells the wronged man to come to the stele.

sentences.l: my-stele the-inscribed let-him-read-aloud-and,
sentences.i: let him read my inscribed stele aloud, and
sentences.n: narûya “my stele” (Harper’s na-ru-i; the final i is -ia “my”) and šaṭram “written, inscribed” (a form of šaṭārum “to write”, the verb of xl 75, as an adjective in the accusative). lištassīma is li + ištassi, the Gt-stem of šasûm “to call, to read aloud” (Harper: “to speak, tell, read”), with -ma. The verb means “read out”: the stele is to be read aloud. The line division at xli 9–10 follows Harper’s transliteration.

sentences.l: my-words weighty let-him-hear-and, my-stele the-matter let-it-show-him,
sentences.i: let him hear my weighty words, and let my stele show him the case,
sentences.n: lišmēma is li + išmē “he hears” (šemûm) + -ma. likallimšu is the precative (li-) of the D-stem of kalāmum “to show” + -šu “to him” (the verb of ukallam “he shall show” in the laws): “let it show him”; the subject is the stele. awātam is “the matter, the case” (his own case, as the next line makes plain). Harper’s e of li-iš-me-ma is slightly damaged on the page; šukuratim is read šūqurātim as at xl 74. One wish is for the ear, the other for the eye: let him hear the words, and let the stele show him his case.

sentences.l: his-case let-him-see, his-heart let-it-be-eased-and,
sentences.i: let him see his own case, and let his heart be eased,
sentences.n: limur is li + imur, from amārum “to see”: “let him see”. dīnšu “his case” (dīnum, with -šu). libbašu “his heart”. linappišma is Harper’s li-na-ab-bi-iš-ma (napašu II “to set at ease”); I normalize it linappiš, the D-stem of napāšum “to breathe, be at ease” (ab and bi can be read ap and pi₂), with -ma “and”. Uncertain: whether the heart is the object (“let him ease his heart”) or the subject (“let his heart be eased”); the sense is the same, and I give the second.

sentences.l: “Hammurabi”-(quoted) the-lord who like a-father begetting to the-people is,
sentences.i: “Hammurabi is a lord who is like a father, a begetter, to the people,
sentences.n: -mi is the particle of quoted speech: it hangs on the first word and says that what follows is spoken; the verb that introduces the speech is liqbīma, “let him say”, at xli 40. The king here writes the praise the reader is to say about him, and it runs through xli 37 as a string of clauses. kīma abim walīdim is “like a father, a begetter” (walīdum, the participle of walādum “to give birth, beget”); ibaššû is the present of bašûm “to be” with the subjunctive -u, because it sits inside a ša-clause: “who is (to the people)”. “Hammurabi” appears without the usual first-person “I”: in this speech he is the one being praised.

sentences.l: to the-word of-Marduk his-lord he-revered-and,
sentences.i: who has revered the word of Marduk his lord,
sentences.n: uštaktitma: Harper’s katatu III,2 “to give reverence to” (us-ta-ak-ti-it): the Š-stem perfect (III,2) with the -ma “and”, “he has shown reverence”; the root is rare and I keep Harper’s reading and gloss. ana awāt Marduk bēlišu “to the word of Marduk his lord”. The unit is the first of a series of praises of the king, each a verb of the 3rd person: revered, attained, made glad, decreed, set right. On the plate xli 25 to 29 are five separate ruled lines (a-na a-wa-at / Marduk be-li-šu / uš-ta-ak-ti with a second row it-ma / ir-ni-ti Marduk / e-li-iš), so Harper’s division stands.

sentences.l: the-victory of-Marduk above and below he-attained,
sentences.i: who has won the victory of Marduk above and below,
sentences.n: irnitti Marduk “the victory of Marduk” (irnittum “victory”, Harper’s irnittu; it has no -m because it stands before its genitive); ikšud is “he reached, attained, won” (kašādum, as in the litany). “Above and below” again means everywhere (as at xl 30–31).

sentences.l: the-heart of-Marduk his-lord he-made-good,
sentences.i: who has gladdened the heart of Marduk his lord,
sentences.n: uṭīb “he made good” is the D-stem of ṭâbum, as at xl 34 and in the litany’s mu-ti-ib li-ib-bi Marduk be-li-šu “gladdener of the heart of Marduk his lord”. The words are the same as that line of the litany. On the plate “be-li-šu u-ti-ib” is one ruled line (xli 33), so Harper’s division stands.

sentences.l: and good-flesh to the-people for ever he-decreed,
sentences.i: who has decreed well-being for the people for ever,
sentences.n: šīram ṭābam “good flesh”, that is, well-being (šīrum, as at xl 33 and in the prologue’s šīr nišī); išīm is “he decreed” (šâmum “to fix, decree”, Harper’s šamu I,1 “to decide”), the verb that fixes destinies. “Good flesh for the people” echoes “the flesh of the land I made good” (xl 33).

sentences.l: and the-land he-set-aright.
sentences.i: and who has put the land in order.”
sentences.n: uštēšir is the perfect of the Š-stem of ešērum “to be straight” (Harper’s III,2 us-te-si-ir; the same form is the Št preterite): “he has set right, put in order”, the verb whose Št infinitive gave šūtešurim in xl 62. This closes the quoted praise. The closing quotation mark follows the quotative -mi of xli 20.

sentences.l: firmly(?) let-him-say-and,
sentences.i: let him say it firmly (?), and
sentences.n: liqbīma is li + iqbi “he says” (qabûm) + -ma, “let him say, and”. Uncertain: danītam. Harper’s glossary lists it as danitu “inscription, code”, and that is all I have; if it is a form of dannum “strong”, it would be an adverbial “firmly”. I give the second (“firmly”) as the English, and `l` follows it; I cannot decide between them: what is said is the praise just quoted.

sentences.l: before Marduk my-lord (and) Zarpanitum my-lady, with his-heart whole let-him-pray-for-me,
sentences.i: let him pray for me before Marduk my lord and Zarpanitum my lady, with his whole heart,
sentences.n: likrubam is li + ikrub “he blesses, prays” (karābum, Harper’s “to bless, to pray”) + the ventive -am “for me, to me”: “let him pray for me”, the precative of the G stem. ina libbišu gamrim “with his whole heart” (libbum “heart”; gamrim, “complete”, Harper’s gamru). Zarpanitum is Marduk’s consort. Harper prints Zar-pa-ni-tum with a single sign zar (his List of Signs no. 183, a box filled with a pine-shaped hatching), and the plate shows one such sign, then pa, ni, tum: five signs after the determinative, not six. Our list has no ZAR; I show the nearest sign, ZA, with the value Zar (TENTATIVE; the real sign is drawn differently from the ZA of Zamama at xl 23). bēltīya “my lady” (bēltum).

sentences.l: the-protective-spirit, the-guardian-spirit, the-gods entering Esagila, the-brickwork of-Esagila, the-igirrû(?) daily,
sentences.i: May the protective spirit, the guardian spirit, the gods who enter Esagila, the brickwork of Esagila, and the igirrê (Harper: “dreams, plans”; unclear), each day
sentences.n: A list of the powers of the temple, five subjects with no “and” between them (the verb comes in the next unit). šēdum and lamassum are two kinds of protective spirit (Harper’s sedu “divinity” and lamassu). ilāni ērībūt Esagila “the gods who enter Esagila” (Harper’s erabu “to enter”; UNCERTAIN: ērībūt could also be a noun). libit Esagila “the brickwork of Esagila”: SIG₄ is the Sumerogram for libittum “brick, brickwork” (Harper’s libittu; the sign is TENTATIVE, added to our list for this line: the plate shows one wide composite sign before É.SAG.ÍL.LA, two clusters of wedges side by side, which I take as the one sign SIG₄, though they could be two). igirrê is Harper’s egirru “dreams, plans” (i-gi-ir-ri-e); I do not know its sense here and leave it as Harper has it, and the whole line is UNCERTAIN. ūmišam “daily” (UD “day” + mi + ša-am; Harper’s ūmišam).

sentences.l: before Marduk my-lord (and) Zarpanitum my-lady may-they-favor.
sentences.i: may they show favor before Marduk my lord and Zarpanitum my lady.
sentences.n: lidammiqū is the 3rd plural precative (li- + dammiq + -ū) of the D-stem of damāqum “to be good”: “may they favor, be gracious” (Harper: damaku II “to favor”). The subject is the five powers of the last unit, so the verb is plural (-ū); the form is written li-dam-mi-ku, KU being read qu₂. The English keeps to Harper’s “to favor”; “for me” is not in the Akkadian, though the sense of the prayer is that.

sentences.l: for the-after, the-future of-days, for whenever:
sentences.i: In the days to come, at any time,
sentences.n: Now the king looks ahead: a new part of the charge. ana warki “for the time after, hereafter” (warkum, “rear, after”; Harper: “after, behind, later”); ṣāt ūmi is “the future of days” (Harper’s satu “future time, eternity”); ūmī is written UD-mi, “day(s)”. The carver wrote A where ṢA was meant (Harper’s a(=ṣa)-at). ana matīma is “whenever, at any time” (Harper’s matima “at the time, when”). The three lines together are an expression for “in all future time”.

sentences.l: the-king who in the-land will-come-to-be, the-words of-justice which on my-stele I-wrote let-him-guard:
sentences.i: may the king who comes to be in the land keep the words of justice that I have written on my stele,
sentences.n: The charge to every later king. šarrum ša ina mātim ibbaššû: the king “who will come to be in the land” (ibbaššû is the N-stem of bašûm “to be”, “to come to be”, in the present with the subjunctive -u). awāt mīšarim is “the words of justice” (awāt, the form before a genitive). ša ina narûya ašṭuru “which I wrote on my stele”, a relative clause with the verb at the end, in the subjunctive. The main verb comes last: liṣṣur is li + iṣṣur, naṣārum “to guard, to observe”: “let him keep”. In xl 79 and here the Sumerogram LUGAL “king” is written with no ending (Harper’s glossary lists these places as the bare LUGAL).

sentences.l: the-case of-the-land which I-gave, the-decisions of-the-land which I-decided, not-may-he-change;
sentences.i: and let him not change the verdicts that I gave for the land or the rulings that I decided for it.
sentences.n: Two relative clauses with the verb in the subjunctive: dīn mātim ša addinu “the case of the land that I gave (rendered)” (nadānum “to give”) and purussê mātim ša aprusu “the decisions of the land that I decided” (parāsum). Then the prohibition: a unakkir is ay + the preterite of the D-stem of nakārum “to change”: “may he not change”. The particle a (Harper: “prohibitive”) makes a negative wish; it is not lā, which would only say “he does not”. I write it ay in the say-line. The same particle appears at xl 92 and next.

sentences.l: my-designs not-may-he-efface.
sentences.i: Let him not efface my designs.
sentences.n: uṣurātīya is “my designs, images” (the same word as in xl 91, in the oblique form -īya); ay ušazziq is ay + the Š preterite of Harper’s nazāqum “to cut off, efface, destroy” (as in mušazziqam, xl 92): “may he not efface”. Harper’s ik for iq is read iq. The part ends in the middle of the charge; it continues in the next part (xli 75 on).
